### Quadratic operators produce inner ideals

**Remember:** One sandwich operator produces a subspace closed under more sandwiches.

*True by definition.* MSC 17C10 (Structure theory for Jordan algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a quadratic Jordan algebra J, a subspace B is an inner ideal if Q(b)c ∈ B for every b ∈ B and c ∈ J. The quadratic operators satisfy Q(Q(a)b) = Q(a)Q(b)Q(a) for all a,b in J.

**Problem.** For every a in a quadratic Jordan algebra, the image of Q(a) is an inner ideal.

**How the definition helps.** The defining identity puts Q(a) last in the order of application, so Q(Q(a)b)c lies in its image (our own). Starting with a binary Jordan product instead requires proving this identity for the associated operators (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Quadratic Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_Jordan_algebra). It says: “For given b, the image of Q(b) is an inner ideal”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Alternating associators force flexibility

**Remember:** An alternating associator vanishes whenever an input repeats.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17D05 (Alternative rings). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The associator measures the difference (xy)z − x(yz). The usual alternative laws say that it vanishes when the first two inputs agree or the last two agree. Equivalently, it is alternating, meaning it vanishes whenever any two inputs agree.

**Problem.** Every alternative algebra satisfies (xy)x = x(yx), even in characteristic two.

**How the definition helps.** The associator is alternating, so it vanishes when its first and third inputs coincide. To see the implication directly, expand the left alternative law at x+y with last input x (our own). The right alternative law kills the term with last inputs x,x, leaving the desired associator zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra). It says: “By definition, a multilinear map is alternating if it vanishes whenever two of its arguments are equal.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Artin’s theorem reverses unit products

**Remember:** Put two units in one associative algebra, then reverse their order.

*True by definition.* MSC 17D05 (Alternative rings). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A unital algebra is alternative if x(xy) = (xx)y and (yx)x = y(xx) for all x,y. Equivalently, by Artin’s theorem, each pair generates an associative subalgebra (our own). A unit has a two-sided multiplicative inverse.

**Problem.** In a finite-dimensional unital alternative algebra over a field, a product of two units is a unit. Its inverse is the product of their inverses in reverse order.

**How the definition helps.** Artin’s theorem makes the unital subalgebra generated by the two units associative (our own). For each unit x, its inverse law makes left multiplication injective on the finite-dimensional subalgebra generated by x and 1 (our own). Surjectivity there supplies a preimage of 1, which the inverse law identifies with x⁻¹ (our own). Both inverses thus lie in the common associative subalgebra, where reverse multiplication gives the inverse (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra). It says: “If x and y are invertible then xy is also invertible with inverse (xy)⁻¹ = y⁻¹x⁻¹.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Commutative alternative algebras associate without three-torsion

**Remember:** Three times the associator vanishes, so rule out three-torsion.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17D05 (Alternative rings). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The associator measures the failure of associativity by A(x,y,z) = (xy)z − x(yz). An algebra is alternative when its associator vanishes whenever two inputs agree. Its additive group has no three-torsion when 3a = 0 forces a = 0.

**Problem.** A commutative alternative algebra without additive three-torsion is associative.

**How the definition helps.** Commutativity makes the cyclic sum of associators zero, while alternation makes its three terms equal (our own). Without three-torsion this forces every associator to vanish. In characteristic three take a commutative algebra with basis x,y,z,u,v,w,t and products xy=u, yz=v, zx=w, uz=t, wy=−t, all others zero (our own). Only permutations of (x,y,z) have nonzero basis associators, equal to t in cyclic order and −t in reverse order (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Cubic norm pairs and hermitian cubic norm structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10426). It says: “For each a,b,c ∈ K, we have 3((ab)c − a(bc)) = 0. Hence, K is associative if K has no 3-torsion.”

**Sources:**

- [Cubic norm pairs and hermitian cubic norm structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10426)

### Pre-Lie left multiplication preserves brackets

**Remember:** Left multiplication takes each bracket to the bracket of operators.

*True by definition.* MSC 17D25 (Lie-admissible algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a vector space with a bilinear product, let L(x) send z to xz. The product is left pre-Lie if \[L(x),L(y)\] = L(xy − yx) for every x,y, using the operator commutator.

**Problem.** In a left pre-Lie algebra, the bracket \[x,y\] = xy − yx makes the algebra a Lie algebra. Left multiplication represents it by linear operators whose commutator equals L(\[x,y\]).

**How the definition helps.** The defining operator equation says exactly that left multiplication preserves brackets. Our own check recovers the usual symmetry by applying both sides to z and rearranging. To prove the Lie bracket identity, expand \[x,\[y,z\]\] + \[y,\[z,x\]\] + \[z,\[x,y\]\]. The terms cancel in pairs of equal associators, the differences between the two ways to group three factors.

**Paper or page:** [Cohomology and Deformations of left-symmetric Rinehart Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.00335v5). It says: “Furthermore, the map adᴸ: L → gl(L) with x ↦ Lₓ gives a representation of the Lie algebra (L,\[·,·\]).”

**Sources:**

- [A. Ben Hassine, T. Chtioui, M. Elhamdadi, S. Mabrouk. Cohomology and Deformations of left-symmetric Rinehart Algebras, Lemma 2.2.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.00335v5)

### Dendriform sums are associative

**Remember:** Add the three split laws to recover the associative law.

*True by definition.* MSC 17A30 (Nonassociative algebras satisfying other identities). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A dendriform dialgebra has two bilinear products ≺ and ≻ with sum ∗. For all x,y,z it satisfies (x≺y)≺z = x≺(y∗z) and (x≻y)≺z = x≻(y≺z). It also satisfies (x ∗ y) ≻ z = x ≻ (y ≻ z).

**Problem.** The sum of the two dendriform operations is associative.

**How the definition helps.** Adding the three defining laws gives the associative law for ∗. Our own comparison starts from the usual test, expanding (x ∗ y) ∗ z and x ∗ (y ∗ z). The three laws already match all terms in these expansions. The work lies in finding operations that satisfy each law separately.

**nLab:** [dendriform algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dendriform+algebra). It says: “The sum of the two binary operations is an associative operation.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Louis Loday. Dialgebras (2001).](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-45328-8_2)

### Zinbiel symmetrization is associative

**Remember:** Rewrite a left pair as the sum of both right orders.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17A30 (Nonassociative algebras satisfying other identities). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Zinbiel algebra has a bilinear product written by juxtaposition, with (xy)z = x(yz + zy). Use the symmetrized product x\*y = xy + yx instead of the original product.

**Problem.** The symmetrized product of a Zinbiel algebra is commutative and associative.

**How the definition helps.** Symmetrizing supplies both orders needed by the Zinbiel rule, so both groupings give x(yz+zy) + y(zx+xz) + z(xy+yx) (our own). For an example over the rationals, take basis a,b,c and products aa=b, ab=c, ba=2c, with all other basis products zero (our own). Only the triple a,a,a gives a nonzero side of the Zinbiel rule, and both sides equal 2c (our own). Yet (aa)a = 2c and a(aa) = c (our own).

**nLab:** [Zinbiel algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Zinbiel+algebra). It says: “A Zinbiel algebra or dual Leibniz algebra (in Vec) is a nonassociative algebra with a product satisfying (xy)z = x(zy + yz),”

**Paper or page:** [On Ternary F-manifold Algebras and their Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13600). It says: “Then (A,·) is a commutative associative algebra, where x·y = x⋄y + y⋄x.”

### Leibniz deformation maps give complements

**Remember:** A complement is a graph, and the bracket must stay on it.

*True by definition.* MSC 17A32 (Leibniz algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a vector space decomposition G ⊕ H of a left Leibniz algebra, with projections p onto G and q onto H. For a linear map r from H to G write s(u) = r(u) + u. Call r a deformation map if p(\[s(u),s(v)\]) = r(q(\[s(u),s(v)\])) for all u,v in H.

**Problem.** The deformation maps correspond to the subalgebras complementary to G as vector spaces.

**How the definition helps.** The component equation says precisely that the graph contains every bracket of two graph elements. Our own comparison starts with a complementary subspace and tests closure there. Projection onto H identifies that subspace with H and gives a unique graph. Computing the two components of the bracket supplies the equation for its map.

**Paper or page:** [Deformation maps in proto-twilled Leibniz algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18599v2). It says: “A linear map r : h → g is a deformation map if and only if the graph Gr(r) = {(r(u), u) \| u ∈ h} is a subalgebra of the Leibniz algebra (G, \[ , \]).”

### Nijenhuis operators preserve deformed products

**Remember:** The Nijenhuis equation says which product the operator preserves.

*True by definition.* MSC 17A36 (Automorphisms, derivations, other operators (nonassociative rings and algebras)). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a linear operator N on an algebra with bilinear multiplication, put x ∗ y = N(x)y + xN(y) − N(xy). Call N a Nijenhuis operator if N(x ∗ y) = N(x)N(y) for every x,y.

**Problem.** Let N be a Nijenhuis operator on a left pre-Jacobi–Jordan algebra. Then x ∗ y is again a left pre-Jacobi–Jordan product, and N is a morphism from the new algebra to the original one.

**How the definition helps.** The Nijenhuis equation gives preservation of the new product immediately. Proposition 5.3 verifies the pre-Jacobi–Jordan identity for the deformed product (our own summary). Preservation alone would only place its identity defect in the kernel of N (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Cohomologies and linear deformations of pre-Jacobi-Jordan algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03076v1). It says: “is left pre-Jacobi-Jordan algebra and N is a morphism”

### Faithful even brackets enable reconstruction

**Remember:** Keep only the even operators that come from odd brackets.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17A40 (Ternary compositions). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Grade an ordinary Lie algebra into even and odd subspaces, with brackets adding degrees modulo two. Its odd part has a ternary operation T(x,y,z) = \[\[x,y\],z\], called its Lie triple product. Reconstruct the even part as the span of the operators z ↦ T(x,y,z).

**Problem.** This construction recovers the original graded Lie algebra if brackets of odd elements span the even part and its action on odd elements is faithful. Faithful means only zero acts by the zero operator.

**How the definition helps.** The spanning condition gives every even action as a sum of triple operators, and faithfulness identifies the even part with their span (our own). Operator commutators recover even brackets by Jacobi, and T(x,y,−) represents the bracket of two odd elements (our own). An abelian graded Lie algebra with a nonzero even part loses that part under reconstruction.

**nLab:** [Lie triple system](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+triple+system). It says: “any abelian ℤ/2-graded Lie algebra (hence with vanishing Lie bracket) converted into a Lie triple system and back into a ℤ/2-graded Lie algebra has a zero-dimensional space of even elements.”

**Sources:**

- [Oleg Smirnov, Imbedding of Lie triple systems into Lie algebras (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jalgebra.2011.06.011)

### Octonions are associative inside a suitably twisted graded category

**Remember:** The octonions are associative once the surrounding category has the right associator.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17A75 (Composition algebras), 18M05, 18A50. arXiv math.RA, math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a standard homogeneous octonion basis indexed by ℤ₂³, define signs ω(a,b) by eₐeᵦ = ω(a,b)eₐ₊ᵦ (our own). Define φ(a,b,c) = ω(a,b)ω(a+b,c)/(ω(b,c)ω(a,b+c)) for all degrees (our own). Use φ as the scalar for rebracketing (U ⊗ V) ⊗ W to U ⊗ (V ⊗ W) on homogeneous tensors (our own).

**Problem.** In the category of ℤ₂³-graded real vector spaces with associator φ, the octonions are an associative algebra (a monoid object).

**How the definition helps.** The ratio of the two bracketings on three homogeneous basis elements is exactly the associator scalar (our own). Bilinearity then gives the monoid associativity law on all inputs (our own).

**nLab:** [Cayley-Dickson construction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cayley-Dickson+construction). It says: “In the case of the octonions, these are better regarded as associative up to a nontrivial cocycle.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Albuquerque, S. Majid, Quasialgebra structure of the octonions, J. Algebra 220 (1999) 188–224](https://doi.org/10.1006/jabr.1998.7850)

### Ihara brackets inherit Jacobi

**Remember:** Take commutators of derivations together with their conjugating elements.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B01 (Identities, free Lie (super)algebras), 11M32. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For each a in the free Lie algebra L on x,y, define the derivation D(a) by D(a)x = 0 and D(a)y = \[y,a\]. Represent a by the pair (a,D(a)) in the semidirect product of L with its derivation algebra (our own).

**Problem.** The Ihara bracket {a,b} = \[a,b\] + D(a)b − D(b)a satisfies the Jacobi identity.

**How the definition helps.** Our own construction realizes the formula as a bracket of pairs, so it inherits Jacobi without expanding a triple bracket. Checking the two generators gives \[D(a),D(b)\] = D({a,b}). This identity proves that the pairs are closed under the bracket.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630). It says: “The pair (𝔣₂, {−,−}) is a Lie algebra.”

**Sources:**

- [Annika Burmester, Niclas Confurius and Ulf Kühn, AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630)

### Paired derivations prove Ihara Jacobi

**Remember:** Pair each Lie element with the derivation it determines.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B01 (Identities, free Lie (super)algebras), 11M32. arXiv math.QA, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For each f in the free Lie algebra on x,y, let dᶠ be the derivation with dᶠ(x) = 0 and dᶠ(y) = \[y,f\]. The Ihara bracket is {f,g} = \[f,g\] + dᶠ(g) − dᵍ(f).

**Problem.** The Ihara bracket satisfies the Jacobi identity.

**How the definition helps.** The bracket is the first coordinate of the ordinary Lie bracket on pairs of Lie elements and derivations. In our own proof, the generator calculation gives \[dᶠ,dᵍ\] = d of the Ihara bracket. Thus the pairs (f,dᶠ) form a subalgebra of the semidirect product, which combines the Lie algebra with its derivations. The generator calculation carries the work that a direct Jacobi expansion would repeat.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “The pair (𝔣₂, {−,−}) is a Lie algebra.”

**Sources:**

- [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1)

### Category O keeps Verma modules while staying abelian and Noetherian

**Remember:** Generate finitely, decompose into weights, and let positive roots act locally finitely.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B10 (Representations of Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras, algebraic theory (weights)), 17B55. arXiv math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤, a Cartan subalgebra 𝔥 and a positive nilpotent subalgebra 𝔫. Category O consists of finitely generated 𝔤-modules that decompose into 𝔥-weight spaces and whose every vector generates a finite-dimensional 𝔫-submodule.

**Problem.** Category O is an abelian category with enough projectives. Every object is Noetherian and has finite-dimensional weight spaces. It contains all Verma modules and all finite-dimensional modules.

**How the definition helps.** The weight and local finiteness conditions admit Verma modules, while finite generation over the Noetherian enveloping algebra controls submodules (our own). The Bernstein–Gelfand–Gelfand structure theorem for category O supplies the remaining finiteness and projectivity assertions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Category O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_O), [Verma module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verma_module). It says: “Each module in category O has finite-dimensional weight spaces. … Each module in category O is a Noetherian module. … O is an abelian category.”

- [Bernstein, I. N., Gelfand, I. M., Gelfand, S. I. (1976). Category of 𝔤-modules. Functional Analysis and Its Applications 10, 87–92.](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01077933)

### The five-cycle gives associator reversal

**Remember:** Forgetting one vertex leaves only the two reversed factors.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B37 (Quantum groups (quantized enveloping algebras) and related deformations). arXiv math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a characteristic-zero group-like series Φ in two primitive noncommuting letters with commutative image one. On five vertices use symmetric edge generators tᵢⱼ, requiring zero incident sum at each vertex and commutation for disjoint edges. The five-cycle condition is Φ(t₁₂,t₂₃)Φ(t₃₄,t₄₅)Φ(t₅₁,t₁₂)Φ(t₂₃,t₃₄)Φ(t₄₅,t₅₁) = 1 (our own).

**Problem.** Every such solution satisfies Φ(x,y)Φ(y,x) = 1.

**How the definition helps.** Forget vertex five, sending t₁₂,t₃₄ to x and t₂₃,t₁₄ to y (our own). The remaining diagonals t₁₃,t₂₄ go to −x−y, respecting vertex sums and disjoint commutations (our own). Each factor involving vertex five has a zero argument and equals one by normalization (our own). The remaining product is Φ(x,y)Φ(y,x) (our own).

**nLab:** [Drinfeld associator](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Drinfeld+associator). It says: “The pentagon equation”

**Sources:**

- [Hidekazu Furusho, Pentagon and hexagon equations, Annals of Mathematics 171 (2010), 545–556](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2010/171-1/p13)

### Torsors give rational associators

**Remember:** The torsor passes from a complex solution to a rational one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B37 (Quantum groups (quantized enveloping algebras) and related deformations). arXiv math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For fixed rational μ ≠ 0, Drinfeld’s associator solutions form a torsor under a prounipotent group over ℚ (our own). A torsor becomes nonempty over an algebraic closure, and the map (g,x) ↦ (gx,x) is an isomorphism onto its square (our own).

**Problem.** A Drinfeld associator over ℚ exists for each nonzero rational μ.

**How the definition helps.** Drinfeld’s complex solution, rescaled to μ, makes the associator torsor geometrically nonempty. Drinfeld’s torsor theorem gives successive lifts controlled by rational vector groups (our own). Such torsors have rational points, so compatible rational lifts in all degrees give the desired series (our own).

**nLab:** [Drinfeld associator](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Drinfeld+associator). It says: “An explicit associator over ℂ was constructed by Drinfeld from the monodromy of a universal version of the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equation.”

**Sources:**

- [Dror Bar-Natan, On associators and the Grothendieck–Teichmuller group I](https://www.math.toronto.edu/drorbn/papers/GT1/GT1.pdf)

### Graphs differentiate Rota–Baxter operators

**Remember:** Differentiate the graph to get the graph of the derivative.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B38 (Yang-Baxter equations and Rota-Baxter operators). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let G act smoothly by automorphisms on H. A smooth map B is a relative Rota–Baxter operator if its graph {(B(h),h) ∣ h ∈ H} is a Lie subgroup of G ⋉ H. For a linear map of the corresponding Lie algebras, require its graph to be a Lie subalgebra of their semidirect product (our own).

**Problem.** The derivative at the identity of a relative Rota–Baxter operator on Lie groups is a relative Rota–Baxter operator on their Lie algebras.

**How the definition helps.** Taking the tangent space at the identity turns the subgroup graph into the graph of the derivative. A Lie subgroup has a Lie subalgebra as its tangent space (our own). The work lies in proving both graph tests equivalent to the usual operator equations (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On the integration of relative Rota-Baxter Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.23547). It says: “Then a smooth map ℬ: H → G is a relative Rota-Baxter operator if and only if the graph Gr(ℬ) = {(ℬ(h), h) \| h ∈ H} is a Lie subgroup”

**Sources:**

- [On the integration of relative Rota-Baxter Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.23547)

### Odd squares need another rule

**Remember:** In characteristic three, one odd triple must vanish on its own.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B50 (Modular Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a parity-graded algebra over a field of characteristic three whose bracket satisfies graded skew symmetry and the graded Jacobi identity. For a Lie superalgebra require also \[\[x,x\],x\] = 0 for every odd element x.

**Problem.** With this extra axiom, each odd x generates the subalgebra spanned by x and \[x,x\].

**How the definition helps.** For odd x the extra axiom kills \[\[x,x\],x\], while the even element \[x,x\] brackets to zero with itself (our own). Without it take odd x,z and even y in characteristic three, setting \[x,x\]=y, \[y,x\]=z and \[x,y\]=−z (our own). Set all other basis brackets to zero (our own). Only the triple x,x,x can contribute to Jacobi, and its three equal terms cancel, although x generates z (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lie superalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_superalgebra). It says: “\[\[x,x\],x\] = 0 for \|x\| = 1 (if 3 is invertible this follows automatically).”

### Coalgebra conjugation preserves Koszul brackets

**Remember:** Conjugate the operator once to transport all its brackets.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B55 (Homological methods in Lie (super)algebras), 81T70. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On the reduced symmetric coalgebra of a graded commutative unital algebra in characteristic zero, let E have n-ary components given by multiplication for every n≥1. For a homogeneous operator D killing 1, let D̃ be the coderivation with unary component D and all higher components zero. The Koszul brackets are the one-output components of K(D) = E⁻¹D̃E (our own).

**Problem.** For operators D and T killing 1, K(\[D,T\]) = \[K(D),K(T)\], where the bracket is the commutator with the graded sign.

**How the definition helps.** Conjugation preserves commutators, so the definition avoids expanding a separate signed product formula for every bracket (our own). The initial extension preserves commutators because terms acting on different factors cancel (our own). Identifying the resulting components with the usual Koszul brackets requires expanding the automorphism and its inverse (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Cumulants, Koszul brackets and homological perturbation theory for commutative BV∞ and IBL∞ algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.14812v1). It says: “is a morphism of graded Lie algebras.”

**Sources:**

- [Ruggero Bandiera, Cumulants, Koszul brackets and homological perturbation theory for commutative BV∞ and IBL∞ algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.14812v1)

### Curvature detects obstructed lifts

**Remember:** Lift once, then test whether the curvature is a differential.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B55 (Homological methods in Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A differential graded Lie algebra has a bracket respecting degrees and a degree-raising differential d satisfying d² = 0 and the signed product rule. A degree-one element a has curvature da + \[a,a\]/2 and is a Maurer–Cartan element when this vanishes. A central extension is a surjective map of such algebras whose kernel brackets to zero with everything.

**Problem.** Let 𝔤̂ → 𝔤 be a central extension of nilpotent differential graded Lie algebras over a field of characteristic zero, with kernel K. Let â be any degree-one lift of a Maurer–Cartan element of 𝔤. Some lift has zero curvature exactly when the curvature of â equals db for some b in K.

**How the definition helps.** Adding a kernel element changes the curvature only by its differential, so subtracting b removes curvature db (our own). The curvature lies in the kernel because its image downstairs is zero (our own). The graded Jacobi identity shows that its differential vanishes (our own). Its class modulo differentials therefore measures the obstruction independently of the chosen lift.

**Paper or page:** [Generalized Positive Energy Representations of Groups of Jets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10390). It says: “\[h\] ∈ H²(K) is independent of the lift”

**Sources:**

- [Generalized Positive Energy Representations of Groups of Jets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10390)

### Lie n-algebras let higher cohomology classify extensions

**Remember:** The ternary bracket is a cocycle, and changing it by a coboundary gives equivalence.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B55 (Homological methods in Lie (super)algebras), 17B56. arXiv math.RA, math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A skeletal Lie 2-algebra has degrees zero and one, zero differential, and brackets of degrees n−2 in arity n satisfying the L∞ identities. Fix the degree-zero Lie bracket and its action on degree one. The remaining bracket takes three degree-zero inputs to degree one (our own).

**Problem.** Over characteristic zero, skeletal Lie 2-algebras with fixed degree-zero Lie algebra 𝔤 and degree-one module M correspond to H³(𝔤;M) up to equivalences fixing both. For finite-dimensional simple 𝔤 the Killing three-form gives the string Lie 2-algebra.

**How the definition helps.** Degree constraints leave only one extra bracket, an alternating map from Λ³𝔤 to M (our own). Its higher Jacobi identity is the three-cocycle condition (our own). The Baez–Crans classification identifies changes by a coboundary with equivalences fixing 𝔤 and M (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology). It says: “any element of the cohomology group Hⁿ⁺¹(𝔤; M) gives an equivalence class of ways to extend the Lie algebra 𝔤 to a "Lie n-algebra" with 𝔤 in grade zero and M in grade n−1.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### L∞ quasi-isomorphisms have quasi-inverses

**Remember:** Test the linear component on cohomology and allow higher components in the inverse.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B55 (Homological methods in Lie (super)algebras), 53D55. arXiv math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In characteristic zero, an L∞ morphism is a degree-zero coalgebra map between the reduced cofree conilpotent symmetric coalgebras on the shifted spaces that intertwines their codifferentials. It is a quasi-isomorphism if its linear component induces an isomorphism on cohomology.

**Problem.** Over a field of characteristic zero, every L∞ quasi-isomorphism F has an L∞ quasi-inverse G, which induces the inverse map on cohomology. So being L∞ quasi-isomorphic is a symmetric relation that needs no zigzags.

**How the definition helps.** Higher components allow homotopy transfer to construct an inverse on minimal models (our own). The quasi-inverse theorem gives a single L∞ morphism back whose linear component induces the inverse on cohomology.

**nLab:** [formal deformation quantization](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/formal+deformation+quantization). It says: “L₁ and L₂ are quasi-isomorphic if there exists M with quasi-isomorphisms L₁ ← M → L₂.”

**Paper or page:** [Lectures on Symplectic Geometry, Poisson Geometry, Deformation Quantization and Quantum Field Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.14662). It says: “If F is a quasi-isomorphism it admits a quasi-inverse, i.e. there is an L∞-morphism G: (g̃,Q̃) → (g,Q) which induces the inverse isomorphism in the corresponding cohomologies.”

**Sources:**

- [Maxim Kontsevich, Deformation quantization of Poisson manifolds, Letters in Mathematical Physics 66 (2003) 157–216](https://doi.org/10.1023/B:MATH.0000027508.00421.bf)

### Translation preserves higher bracket identities

**Remember:** Changing the origin does not change the square.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B55 (Homological methods in Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a shifted graded space over a characteristic-zero field, a curved L∞ structure is a formal degree-one vector field Q satisfying Q² = 0. Use a complete separated descending filtration in which each bracket sends inputs of filtration orders i₁,…,iₙ to order at least their sum. For v of degree zero and filtration at least one, the twist is the translated field Qᵛ(x) = Q(v+x) (our own).

**Problem.** The translated vector field defines a curved higher Lie algebra on the same space.

**How the definition helps.** Translation conjugates the operator, so its square stays zero (our own). This proves all the new higher bracket identities at once (our own). The work goes into comparing the translated Taylor coefficients with the usual bracket formulas (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A Lie theoretic approach to the twisting procedure and Maurer-Cartan simplicial sets over arbitrary rings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16706v1). It says: “The twisted differential Qᵛ is a coderivation and squares to zero.”

**Sources:**

- [Niek de Kleijn, Felix Wierstra, A Lie theoretic approach to the twisting procedure and Maurer-Cartan simplicial sets over arbitrary rings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16706v1)

### Twisting turns solutions into flatness

**Remember:** Move the origin to a zero of the vector field.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B55 (Homological methods in Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A curved L∞ structure on a shifted characteristic-zero space is a formal degree-one vector field Q satisfying Q² = 0. Assume a complete separated descending filtration with brackets of filtration order at least the sum of input orders. For degree-zero v of positive filtration, the twist has field Q(v+x) and is flat when its constant term vanishes (our own).

**Problem.** The translated higher Lie algebra is flat exactly when v satisfies the Maurer–Cartan equation, the vanishing of the sum of the bracket terms at v.

**How the definition helps.** The new constant term is Q evaluated at v, which is the Maurer–Cartan series (our own). The work goes into justifying the translation in the filtration and identifying its Taylor coefficients with the twisted brackets (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A Lie theoretic approach to the twisting procedure and Maurer-Cartan simplicial sets over arbitrary rings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16706v1). It says: “is flat if and only if v is a Maurer-Cartan element.”

**Sources:**

- [Niek de Kleijn, Felix Wierstra, A Lie theoretic approach to the twisting procedure and Maurer-Cartan simplicial sets over arbitrary rings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16706v1)

### Characteristic zero excludes simple modular modules with nonzero first cohomology

**Remember:** In characteristic p the Casimir can vanish, and Whitehead's lemmas fail.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B50. arXiv math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra in characteristic zero, choose a basis eᵢ and its Killing-dual basis eⁱ. The Killing-form Casimir is ∑ᵢ eᵢeⁱ in the enveloping algebra (our own).

**Problem.** For finite-dimensional semisimple 𝔤 in characteristic zero and every finite-dimensional module V, H¹(𝔤,V) = H²(𝔤,V) = 0. Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p &gt; 3, the nontrivial simple 𝔰𝔩₃-module L(p−2,1) has nonzero H¹.

**How the definition helps.** The Casimir acts invertibly on nontrivial irreducibles in characteristic zero, a step in the proof of Whitehead’s lemmas (our own). In the modular example its normalized scalar is 2p²/3, which vanishes in the field (our own). The cited computation gives nonzero H¹ there.

**Paper or page:** [Cohomology of 𝔰𝔩₃ and 𝔤𝔩₃ with Coefficients in Simple Modules and Weyl Modules in Positive Characteristics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16142). It says: “Let 𝔤=𝔰𝔩₃(k) and M=L(p−2,1). Then, Hⁿ(𝔤,M)=0, except for the following cases: (i) H¹(𝔤,L(p−2,1))≅H⁷(𝔤,L(p−2,1))≅L(1,0)⁽¹⁾”

**Sources:**

- [Cohomology of 𝔰𝔩₃ and 𝔤𝔩₃ with Coefficients in Simple Modules and Weyl Modules in Positive Characteristics, arXiv:2203.16142](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16142)

### Cyclic homology makes the homology of matrix Lie algebras statable

**Remember:** Primitive homology of matrices is cyclic homology shifted by one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 19D55. arXiv math.KT, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a unital algebra A over a characteristic-zero field, take Hochschild chains A⊗⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ in degree n with their Hochschild boundary. Identify each tensor with its cyclic rotation multiplied by (−1)ⁿ. The homology of this quotient is HC\*(A), and 𝔤𝔩(A) is the union under upper-left block inclusions (our own).

**Problem.** Let A be a unital associative algebra over a field of characteristic zero. Then H\*(𝔤𝔩(A);k) is a Hopf algebra whose primitive part in degree n is HCₙ₋₁(A) (Loday–Quillen, Tsygan).

**How the definition helps.** Cyclic coinvariants put single cycles in one complex for every matrix size (our own). The Loday–Quillen–Tsygan theorem identifies the shifted homology of this complex with stable primitive Lie homology (our own).

**nLab:** [Loday-Quillen-Tsygan theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Loday-Quillen-Tsygan+theorem), [Lie algebra homology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+homology). It says: “states that for any associative algebra, A in characteristic zero, the Lie algebra homology H•(𝔤𝔩(A)) of the infinite general linear Lie algebra 𝔤𝔩(A) with coefficients in A is, up to a degree shift, the exterior algebra”

**Sources:**

- [J.-L. Loday and D. Quillen, Cyclic homology and the Lie algebra homology of matrices, Comment. Math. Helv. 59 (1984) 565–591](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02566367)

### Cyclic homology names the center of universal current algebras

**Remember:** The universal center of 𝔤 ⊗ A is one-forms modulo exact forms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B67, 19D55. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let A be a commutative complex algebra. Its first cyclic homology HC₁(A) is Ω¹(A)/dA, the Kähler 1-forms (formal sums of a db) modulo exact forms. The current algebra 𝔤 ⊗ A of a finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra 𝔤 has bracket \[x⊗a, y⊗b\] = \[x,y\]⊗ab.

**Problem.** For finite-dimensional simple complex 𝔤 and a unital commutative complex algebra A, the universal central extension of 𝔤 ⊗ A has kernel HC₁(A) = Ω¹(A)/dA. For A = ℂ\[t,t⁻¹\], the class of t⁻¹dt spans the kernel, giving the affine algebra without its degree derivation.

**How the definition helps.** Cyclic homology gives the kernel a name that works for every A at once. So the theorem is one formula instead of a computation for each algebra. The cocycle is (x⊗a, y⊗b) ↦ (x,y)·(a db) in Ω¹(A)/dA, with (x,y) the Killing form (our own). The work went into Kassel's proof that this cocycle is universal.

**Paper or page:** [Affine super Yangians and deformed double current superalgebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07328). It says: “let HC₁(A) denote the first cyclic homology group of A. The universal central extension 𝔤(A) of … is given by 𝔤(A) ≃ 𝔤 ⊗ A ⊕ HC₁(A) if 𝔤 is not of type A(n,n)”

**Sources:**

- [C. Kassel, Kähler differentials and coverings of complex simple Lie algebras extended over a commutative algebra, J. Pure Appl. Algebra 34 (1984) 265–275](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-4049(84)90040-9)

### Finite dimension excludes affine algebras without Levi decomposition

**Remember:** Commuting opposite loops acquire a central bracket that no section can remove.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B67. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For finite-dimensional simple complex 𝔤 with Killing form ( , ), form its loop algebra 𝔤 ⊗ ℂ\[t,t⁻¹\]. Its affine central extension adds a central basis vector c with bracket \[x⊗tᵐ,y⊗tⁿ\] = \[x,y\]⊗tᵐ⁺ⁿ + mδₘ₊ₙ,₀(x,y)c (our own).

**Problem.** Every finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero is the semidirect product of a semisimple subalgebra and its radical. The finiteness condition is needed: the affine Lie algebra has radical equal to its one-dimensional center, but no complement.

**How the definition helps.** Choose h with (h,h) ≠ 0. The commuting loops h⊗t and h⊗t⁻¹ have nonzero cocycle value, whereas every coboundary vanishes on commuting pairs (our own). Thus the extension cannot split, and its infinite dimension excludes it from Levi’s theorem (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Levi decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi_decomposition). It says: “affine Lie algebras have a radical consisting of their center, but cannot be written as a semidirect product of the center and another Lie algebra.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### H² with adjoint coefficients counts deformations, so semisimple Lie algebras are rigid

**Remember:** Linearize Jacobi and divide out infinitesimal basis changes.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B20. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A first-order deformation of a Lie bracket μ is a bracket μ+tφ over k\[t\]/(t²) reducing to μ modulo t. Two deformations are equivalent if a linear change of basis reducing to the identity modulo t intertwines them.

**Problem.** A finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero is rigid. That is, its orbit under change of basis is open in the variety of all Lie brackets of that dimension.

**How the definition helps.** Linearizing Jacobi gives the adjoint two-cocycles, and infinitesimal basis changes give the coboundaries (our own). Whitehead’s second lemma kills their quotient for semisimple 𝔤 (our own). The Nijenhuis–Richardson rigidity criterion then gives an open orbit.

**Paper or page:** [Deformations and rigidity in varieties of Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.09670). It says: “Let 𝕂 be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and let ℒₙ=Lₙ(𝕂), with the structure of affine algebraic variety. Given μ ∈ ℒₙ, if H²(μ,μ)=0, then μ is rigid in ℒₙ.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Nijenhuis and R. W. Richardson, Cohomology and deformations in graded Lie algebras, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 72 (1966) 1–29](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9904-1966-11401-5)

### Relative cohomology as Ext of (𝔤,K)-modules forces matching infinitesimal characters

**Remember:** Cohomology needs the infinitesimal character of the trivial representation.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 22E47, 22E46. arXiv math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let G be a connected real reductive group with maximal compact subgroup K, and write 𝔤 for its complexified Lie algebra. Define Hⁿ(𝔤,K;V) as Extⁿ from the trivial module to V in the category of complex (𝔤,K)-modules.

**Problem.** If an irreducible (𝔤,K)-module π has nonzero (𝔤,K)-cohomology, then π has the same infinitesimal character as the trivial representation (Wigner's lemma). For unitary π this is part of the Vogan–Zuckerman classification of cohomological representations.

**How the definition helps.** Each central element acts on Ext through either argument with the same result (our own). Different infinitesimal characters give different scalars for some central element, forcing Ext to vanish (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Limit Multiplicity For Unitary Groups and The Stable Trace Formula](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.09834). It says: “The group G has finitely many cohomological representations π, and Hⁱ(𝔤, K; π) ≠ 0 if and only if: (i) π has the infinitesimal character of the trivial representation of G, and;”

**Sources:**

- [Limit Multiplicity For Unitary Groups and The Stable Trace Formula, arXiv:2105.09834](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.09834)

### Relative cohomology makes the Hochschild–Serre factorization one tensor product

**Remember:** Cohomology of 𝔰 ⋉ 𝔯 is H(𝔰) times the relative part.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 18G40. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Relative cochains in degree n are the 𝔰-equivariant linear maps Λⁿ(𝔤/𝔰) → M. Pull them back to alternating cochains on 𝔤 and restrict the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential to them. Their cohomology is H\*(𝔤,𝔰;M).

**Problem.** Let 𝔤 = 𝔰 ⋉ 𝔯 be finite-dimensional over a field of characteristic zero, with 𝔰 semisimple, and let M be a finite-dimensional 𝔤-module. Then H\*(𝔤;M) ≅ H\*(𝔰;k) ⊗ H\*(𝔤,𝔰;M) (Hochschild and Serre).

**How the definition helps.** Relative cochains identify with 𝔰-invariant cochains on 𝔯 (our own). Complete reducibility lets invariants commute with cohomology here (our own). The Hochschild–Serre factorization theorem identifies the other factor as H\*(𝔰;k) and gives the stated tensor product (our own).

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “Then the invariants in the Lie algebra cohomology of 𝔞 (either with respect to 𝔥 or all of 𝔤) coincide with the relative Lie algebra cohomology”

**Paper or page:** [Cohomology of perfect Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.14952). It says: “Let 𝔤=𝔰⋉V with 𝔰=𝔰𝔩₂(ℂ), V=Vₘ and k≥0. Then we have Hᵏ(𝔤,𝔤) ≅ ⊕<sub>i+j=k</sub> Hⁱ(𝔰,ℂ)⊗Hʲ(V,𝔤)<sup>𝔰</sup>”

**Sources:**

- [G. Hochschild and J.-P. Serre, Cohomology of Lie algebras, Ann. of Math. 57 (1953) 591–603](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969740)

### Relative Lie algebra cohomology makes Matsushima's formula for locally symmetric spaces statable

**Remember:** Betti numbers of Γ∖G/K count representations weighted by their relative cohomology.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 22E40, 11F75. arXiv math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take connected semisimple G with maximal compact K and torsion-free cocompact lattice Γ, and complexify the Lie algebras 𝔤 and 𝔨. Relative cohomology uses the complex of K-equivariant maps Λⁿ(𝔤/𝔨) → V with its Chevalley–Eilenberg differential. For a unitary representation take its smooth K-finite vectors (our own).

**Problem.** The cohomology H\*(Γ∖G/K; ℂ) is the sum, over irreducible unitary π, of m(π,Γ) copies of H\*(𝔤,K;π). Here m(π,Γ) is the multiplicity of π in L²(Γ∖G) (Matsushima).

**How the definition helps.** Differential forms on Γ∖G/K give relative cochains with smooth function coefficients on Γ∖G (our own). Matsushima’s theorem passes the discrete representation decomposition to cohomology, with each contributing representation counted by its multiplicity (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Limit Multiplicity For Unitary Groups and The Stable Trace Formula](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.09834). It says: “Let hⁱₖ(𝔭ⁿ) denote the dimension of the subspace of Hⁱ(Γ(𝔭ⁿ), 𝐂) coming from the (𝔤,K)-cohomology of the representation πₖ.”

**Sources:**

- [Y. Matsushima, A formula for the Betti numbers of compact locally symmetric Riemannian manifolds, J. Differential Geom. 1 (1967) 99–109](https://doi.org/10.4310/jdg/1214427883)

### Relative Lie algebra cohomology makes van Est's comparison theorem statable

**Remember:** Continuous group cohomology equals Lie algebra cohomology relative to compact directions.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 22E41. arXiv math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For Lie algebras 𝔨 ⊂ 𝔤 and a finite-dimensional 𝔤-module V, use the alternating 𝔨-equivariant maps from (𝔤/𝔨)ⁿ to V in degree n. Relative cohomology is the cohomology of these cochains with the induced Chevalley–Eilenberg differential.

**Problem.** Let G be a connected Lie group with maximal compact subgroup K, and V a finite-dimensional continuous G-module. Then the continuous cohomology of G with coefficients in V is H\*(𝔤,𝔨;V), which is H\*(𝔤;V) when G is contractible (van Est).

**How the definition helps.** The relative complex is exactly the complex of G-invariant V-valued forms on the contractible space G/K. So relative cohomology is the right target for differentiating group cochains (our own). The work went into van Est's proof that the differentiation map is an isomorphism, which uses the contractibility of G/K.

**nLab:** [van Est isomorphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/van+Est+isomorphism). It says: “The content of a van Est isomorphism is that the canonical comparison map from Lie group cohomology to Lie algebra cohomology (by differentiation) is an isomorphism whenever the Lie group is sufficiently connected.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The dot action makes Kostant's theorem on nilradical cohomology one formula

**Remember:** Each degree of nilradical cohomology lists the dot images of λ once.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B10. arXiv math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Choose positive roots making the parabolic standard and let ρ be their half-sum. Define w·λ = w(λ+ρ) − ρ. For Weyl groups W of 𝔤 and Wₗ of its Levi factor, Wᴾ contains the minimum-length representative of each coset wWₗ.

**Problem.** Let V(λ) be an irreducible finite-dimensional 𝔤-module. In degree q, the cohomology of 𝔲 in V(λ) is the sum of the irreducible 𝔩-modules of highest weight w⁻¹·λ, for w in Wᴾ of length q (Kostant).

**How the definition helps.** The dot action turns the answer into a list indexed by Weyl group elements of a given length, with no case analysis. For the Borel subalgebra this gives one weight w·λ for each w of length q. The work went into Kostant's Laplacian on the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex of 𝔲, whose kernel is computed with the Casimir element.

**Paper or page:** [Uniform twisted homological stability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.00354). It says: “H<sup>q</sup>(𝔲;V(λ)) = ⊕<sub>w ∈ W<sup>P</sup>, ℓ(w)=q</sub> V\_𝔩(w⁻¹•λ), where V\_𝔩(μ) denotes the irreducible representation of 𝔩 of highest weight μ.”

**Sources:**

- [B. Kostant, Lie algebra cohomology and the generalized Borel–Weil theorem, Ann. of Math. 74 (1961) 329–387](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970237)

### Unimodularity gives Lie algebra cohomology Poincaré duality

**Remember:** Trace zero makes the top exterior power a trivial module.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B30. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A finite-dimensional Lie algebra 𝔤 is unimodular if tr(ad x) = 0 for every x. Equivalently, 𝔤 acts trivially on the top exterior power Λᵈ𝔤, where d = dim 𝔤.

**Problem.** For a unimodular Lie algebra 𝔤 of dimension d over a field k, Hⁱ(𝔤;k) is dual to Hᵈ⁻ⁱ(𝔤;k), and the top cohomology is k. Without unimodularity this fails: for the two-dimensional algebra with \[x,y\] = y, H⁰ = k but H² = 0.

**How the definition helps.** Unimodularity says that the dualizing module of U(𝔤), Λᵈ𝔤\* with its 𝔤-action, is trivial, so the duality in the quote becomes Poincaré duality (our own). In the two-dimensional example, d(y\*) = −x\*∧y\*, so the top form is exact and H² = 0 (our own computation). The work went into showing that U(𝔤) is a duality algebra, using the Chevalley–Eilenberg resolution.

**Paper or page:** [Kurosh theorem for certain Koszul Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03034). It says: “Let D be the right A-module Hⁿ(A,A). Then for every left A-module M there holds the following homological duality Hⁱ(A,M)≃Torᴬₙ₋ᵢ(D,M).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Vanishing H¹ and H² recognize the Virasoro algebra as universal

**Remember:** A perfect extension with no further extensions is the universal one.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B68. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A central extension p from 𝔢 onto 𝔤 is universal if every central extension q onto 𝔤 admits exactly one Lie map f with qf=p. Over a field this holds when 𝔢 is perfect and H²(𝔢;k) vanishes (our own).

**Problem.** In characteristic zero, the Virasoro algebra is the universal central extension of the two-sided Witt algebra of polynomial vector fields on the circle. Its kernel is one-dimensional.

**How the definition helps.** Pulling any central extension back to the Virasoro algebra gives a split extension by the H² vanishing (our own). Perfectness makes the resulting lift unique, since two lifts differ by a map from the abelianization (our own). The quoted vanishing theorem gives both conditions, and the Virasoro extension has one central generator (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Virasoro algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virasoro_algebra). It says: “the Virasoro algebra is a complex Lie algebra and the unique nontrivial central extension of the Witt algebra.”

**Paper or page:** [Lie algebras whose derivation algebras are simple](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15560). It says: “Let 𝒱 denote the Virasoro algebra over a field 𝔽 of characteristic zero. Then H¹(𝒱,𝔽)=H²(𝒱,𝔽)=0. In particular, the Virasoro algebra 𝒱 is a universal central extension of the two-sided Witt algebra 𝒲.”

**Sources:**

- [I. M. Gel'fand and D. B. Fuks, The cohomologies of the Lie algebra of the vector fields in a circle, Funct. Anal. Appl. 2 (1968) 342–343](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01075687)

### Vanishing second Lie algebra cohomology lets projective representations lift

**Remember:** No real H², no projective phases after passing to the universal cover.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 22E70, 22D12. arXiv math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A continuous projective unitary representation on a Hilbert space H is a continuous homomorphism to U(H)/U(1), using the strong operator topology and quotient topology. Here U(1) acts by scalar multiples of the identity.

**Problem.** For a connected Lie group G with H²(𝔤;ℝ) = 0, every continuous projective unitary representation lifts to a unitary representation on the universal cover.

**How the definition helps.** Bargmann’s theorem constructs a Lie group circle extension from the projective action. Vanishing H² splits its Lie algebra extension, and the section integrates on the universal cover (our own). For ℝ²ⁿ with n ≥ 1, the Heisenberg representation gives a nonzero alternating cocycle that prevents lifting (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Projective representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_representation). It says: “Bargmann's theorem states that if the second Lie algebra cohomology group H²(𝔤; ℝ) of 𝔤 is trivial, then every projective unitary representation of G can be de-projectivized after passing to the universal cover.”

**Sources:**

- [V. Bargmann, On unitary ray representations of continuous groups, Ann. of Math. 59 (1954) 1–46](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969831)
- [D. J. Simms, A short proof of Bargmann's criterion for the lifting of projective representations of Lie groups, Rep. Math. Phys. 2 (1971) 283–287](https://doi.org/10.1016/0034-4877(71)90011-5)

### Manin triples expose duality

**Remember:** Switch the two halves of the Manin triple to get the dual.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B62 (Lie bialgebras; Lie coalgebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Manin triple consists of a Lie algebra with a nondegenerate symmetric invariant bilinear form and two Lie subalgebras complementary as vector spaces. The form vanishes on each subalgebra separately and satisfies B(\[x,y\],z) = B(x,\[y,z\]) for all x,y,z.

**Problem.** The dual of a finite-dimensional Lie bialgebra is a Lie bialgebra.

**How the definition helps.** Exchanging the two subalgebras preserves every condition on a Manin triple and puts the dual space first (our own). The work lies in proving that Manin triples describe precisely the compatible brackets of finite-dimensional Lie bialgebras (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Manin triple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manin_triple). It says: “There is an equivalence of categories between finite-dimensional Manin triples and finite-dimensional Lie bialgebras.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Free orbits preserve irreducibility

**Remember:** A free module orbit has no stabilizer labels to split it.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let a finite group G act by automorphisms on a countable-dimensional simple complex vertex algebra V. For a V-module M, twist its action by precomposition with each g in G. Its orbit is free if the twist is isomorphic to M only for g equal to the identity.

**Problem.** A simple V-module stays simple over the subalgebra fixed by G exactly when its orbit is free.

**How the definition helps.** The restriction theorem labels summands by simple modules for the twisted stabilizer algebra. A trivial stabilizer gives one label of multiplicity one (our own). For the rank-one lattice algebra with sign involution, the vacuum module splits into nonzero even and odd eigenspaces over the fixed algebra (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Orbifold theory for vertex algebras and Galois correspondence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.09474v1), [Orbifold theory for vertex algebras and Galois correspondence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.09474v1). It says: “Then M is an irreducible Vᴳ-module if and only if Gₘ = {1}.”

**Sources:**

- [Chongying Dong, Li Ren, Chao Yang, Orbifold theory for vertex algebras and Galois correspondence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.09474v1)

### Inversion reverses the dual twist

**Remember:** Reverse the coordinate, and you reverse the twist.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a lower-bounded twisted module M with finite-dimensional weight spaces, its graded dual is the direct sum of their duals. Its field for a homogeneous state a of integral weight h is the transpose of Yᴹ(exp(zL₁)(−z⁻²)ʰa,1/z) (our own).

**Problem.** Let g be a finite-order automorphism of a complex vertex operator algebra. If fields on M acquire the twist g around zero, the fields on its graded dual have twist g⁻¹.

**How the definition helps.** In our own argument inversion reverses a loop around zero, so it reverses the twist. The state correction contributes only integral powers of z. Transposing modes alone would miss the reversal. The theorem also verifies that the new fields satisfy the twisted module identities.

**Paper or page:** [Twisted regular representations and bimodules in vertex operator algebra theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16464v1). It says: “(M′, Y\[M\]′) is a g⁻¹-twisted module”

**Sources:**

- [Yiyi Zhu, Twisted regular representations and bimodules in vertex operator algebra theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16464v1)

### Jet coordinates generate Li’s graded algebra

**Remember:** Negative modes become products of derivatives of degree-zero classes.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a complex vertex algebra, assign weight k to every mode with index −1−k for k ≥ 0. Let F(p) be the span of all strings of these modes applied to states with total mode weight at least p, including empty strings. Degree p of Li’s graded algebra is F(p)/F(p+1).

**Problem.** Let R = F(0)/F(1) be the degree-zero part. The jet algebra of R, made by adjoining formal derivatives subject to all differentiated relations, maps onto the graded algebra by a map that preserves products and derivatives.

**How the definition helps.** Every spanning string becomes a product of derivatives of degree-zero classes (our own). The mode −1−k of a state equals the mode −1 of its kth derivative divided by k! (our own). Li’s filtration theorem supplies the differential commutative algebra structure, so the jet algebra’s universal property gives a surjection (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Li filtrations of SUSY vertex algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05734v1), [Li filtrations of SUSY vertex algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05734v1). It says: “then φ extends to a surjective morphism”

**Sources:**

- [Shintarou Yanagida, Li filtrations of SUSY vertex algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05734v1)

### Li’s degree zero is Poisson

**Remember:** The mode −2 quotient is the degree-zero part of the graded Poisson structure.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a complex vertex algebra, assign weight k to every mode with index −1−k for k ≥ 0. Let F(p) be the span of all strings of these modes applied to states with total mode weight at least p, including empty strings. Degree p of Li’s graded algebra is F(p)/F(p+1).

**Problem.** The quotient by the span of mode −2 products is a Poisson algebra. Mode −1 gives its commutative product, and mode zero gives a Lie bracket satisfying the product rule.

**How the definition helps.** Li’s filtration theorem gives a vertex Poisson algebra on the associated graded space (our own). In degree zero its product and zero-mode bracket satisfy the ordinary Poisson identities (our own). The identification of F(1) with the span of mode −2 products transfers both operations to the stated quotient (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Zhu algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhu_algebra). It says: “The multiplication of the C₂-algebra is commutative”

**Paper or page:** [Li filtrations of SUSY vertex algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05734v1). It says: “is equal to the degree zero subspace E₀(V)/E₁(V) = V/E₁(V) ⊂ gr\[E\] V of the Li filtration.”

**Sources:**

- [Shintarou Yanagida, Li filtrations of SUSY vertex algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05734v1)

### Li’s graded fields lose poles

**Remember:** Derivative degree makes singular products vanish in the leading operations.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a complex vertex algebra, assign weight k to every mode with index −1−k for k ≥ 0. Let F(p) be the span of all strings of these modes applied to states with total mode weight at least p, including empty strings. Degree p of Li’s graded algebra is F(p)/F(p+1).

**Problem.** In the vertex algebra formed from these successive quotients, every field has zero singular part.

**How the definition helps.** Li’s filtration estimate puts the mth mode of inputs from F(r),F(s) in F(r+s−m) for m ≥ 0 (our own). The graded field takes its class one degree earlier, modulo this very subspace (our own). Thus every pole coefficient vanishes (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Li filtrations of SUSY vertex algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05734v1), [Li filtrations of SUSY vertex algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05734v1). It says: “is commutative if and only if a₍ₘ∣ᴹ₎b ∈ E\[r+s−m\]”

**Sources:**

- [Shintarou Yanagida, Li filtrations of SUSY vertex algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05734v1)

### Local constancy makes fields commute

**Remember:** Constant disc maps leave no room for poles.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A holomorphic prefactorization algebra on the plane is locally constant if the structure map for every inclusion of open discs is an isomorphism.

**Problem.** For such a locally constant algebra, the associated vertex algebra is commutative. This means all coefficients of negative powers in its fields vanish.

**How the definition helps.** Local constancy identifies the disc spaces and lets the two-disc product extend across coincident insertion points (our own). The vertex algebra construction reads the negative field coefficients from the poles of this product, so they vanish (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A note on vertex algebras and Costello-Gwilliam factorization algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00412v2), [A note on vertex algebras and Costello-Gwilliam factorization algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00412v2). It says: “then the vertex algebra 𝐕(ℱ) is commutative.”

**Sources:**

### Rationality excludes triplet character anomalies

**Remember:** Rationality makes every admissible module split into simple modules.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a simple self-dual vertex operator algebra of CFT type. It is C₂-cofinite if all mode −2 products span a subspace of finite codimension. It is rational if every admissible module is a direct sum of simple modules.

**Problem.** For such a rational, C₂-cofinite algebra, the simple characters span a space invariant under τ ↦ τ+1 and τ ↦ −1/τ. Here the character of M is the graded trace of q raised to L₀−c/24, with q = exp(2πiτ).

**How the definition helps.** Rationality excludes the triplet example where the span of simple characters fails to close under inversion. Our own illustration uses the algebra W(2), which satisfies the finite codimension condition. Inversion introduces a function containing τ times a theta-function derivative outside the character span. Zhu’s modular invariance theorem proves closure under the stated hypotheses.

**Wikipedia:** [Zhu algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhu_algebra). It says: “the triplet vertex operator algebra is C₂-cofinite but not rational.”

**Paper or page:** [Character Vectors of Strongly Regular Vertex Operator Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.04616v3), [Character Vectors of Strongly Regular Vertex Operator Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.04616v3). It says: “Then 𝔠𝔥\[V\] is a right Γ-submodule of 𝔉.”

### Sewing proves field associativity

**Remember:** Two sewings of one sphere give two expansions of one operation.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** At central charge zero, the sewing axiom assigns to each admissible gluing of marked, locally coordinated spheres the composite of their multilinear operations. Composition sums over the intermediate weight spaces at the glued punctures (our own).

**Problem.** Take states u, v, w and pair the output with any graded dual vector. The product Y(u,z₁)Y(v,z₂)w and iterate Y(Y(u,z₁ − z₂)v,z₂)w agree wherever \|z₁\| &gt; \|z₂\| &gt; \|z₁ − z₂\| &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** Our own argument obtains both expressions by sewing the same four-point sphere in two ways. The inequalities put both sewing expansions inside their convergence regions. Huang’s equivalence theorem supplies convergence and identifies the geometric operations with the formal fields.

**nLab:** [vertex operator algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/vertex+operator+algebra). It says: “Composition of such spheres is by gluing along punctures.”

**Sources:**

- [Yi-Zhi Huang, Two-Dimensional Conformal Geometry and Vertex Operator Algebras](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-4276-5)

### Zhu’s algebra detects endomorphisms

**Remember:** An endomorphism of a simple module is determined at its bottom.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For homogeneous a of weight h in V and any b in V, put F(z) = (1+z)ʰY(a,z)b. Zhu’s algebra is V modulo the span of all residues of F(z)/z². Its product takes the class of the residue of F(z)/z and extends bilinearly (our own).

**Problem.** Let M be a simple admissible module, graded by nonnegative integers compatibly with the field modes, with nonzero degree zero. Restriction identifies its module endomorphism ring with the endomorphism ring of its degree-zero space over Zhu’s algebra.

**How the definition helps.** Zhu’s induction theorem recovers a simple admissible module from its nonzero bottom space (our own). Restriction is injective because the bottom generates M (our own). Functorial induction and passage to the canonical simple quotient extend every bottom endomorphism to M (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Endomorphism property of vertex operator algebras over arbitrary fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.16573v2), [Endomorphism property of vertex operator algebras over arbitrary fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.16573v2). It says: “End\[V\](M) ≅ End\[A(V)\](M(0)).”

**Sources:**

- [Chao Yang, Jianqi Liu, Endomorphism property of vertex operator algebras over arbitrary fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.16573v2)

### Quadratic operators preserve Jordan invertibility

**Remember:** Three invertible operators compose to give another invertible operator.

*True by definition.* MSC 17C05 (Identities and free Jordan structures). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a unital quadratic Jordan algebra, each element x gives a linear operator U(x) depending quadratically on x. The fundamental identity U(U(x)y) = U(x)U(y)U(x) is one of the axioms. Call x invertible if U(x) is an invertible linear map.

**Problem.** In a unital quadratic Jordan algebra, U(x)y is invertible whenever x and y are invertible.

**How the definition helps.** Our own argument is that the fundamental identity expresses U(U(x)y) as a product of invertible operators. The work is to prove the fundamental identity from the usual bilinear Jordan product when two is invertible. In the quadratic definition it is already an axiom.

**nLab:** [quadratic Jordan algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quadratic+Jordan+algebra). It says: “the fundamental identity holds: U(U(v) w) = U(v) U(w) U(v) for all v,w ∈ V,”

**Sources:**

- [Kevin McCrimmon. A Taste of Jordan Algebras (2004).](https://doi.org/10.1007/B97489)

### Jordan pairs accommodate rectangular matrices

**Remember:** Put matrices of the opposite shape in the middle.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17C50 (Jordan structures associated with other structures). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Jordan pair has two spaces with trilinear products {abc}. The outer inputs and output occupy either space, and the middle input occupies the other. Each product is symmetric in its outer inputs. Writing D(a,b)c = {abc}, require \[D(a,b),D(x,y)\] = D({abx},y) − D(x,{bay}) for all a,x in either space and b,y opposite.

**Problem.** Over a field of characteristic zero, the spaces of m-by-n and n-by-m matrices form a Jordan pair with triple products abc + cba.

**How the definition helps.** The opposite shapes let both products return to the space of their outer inputs. The theorem that transfers the Lie bracket identities to Jordan pairs does the work. Our own check places the rectangular matrices in opposite off-diagonal blocks of square matrices. The double bracket on these blocks is abc + cba.

**nLab:** [Jordan pair](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jordan+pair). It says: “it makes sense when a and c are m × n matrices and b is an n × m matrix, or vice versa.”

**Sources:**

- [Ottmar Loos. Jordan Pairs (1975).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0080843)

### In a formally real algebra, sums of squares give a partial order

**Remember:** Zero is a sum of squares only in the trivial way.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17C55 (Finite-dimensional structures of Jordan algebras), 17C90, 13J25. arXiv math.RA, math.OA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An algebra is formally real if, for every finite list x₁,…,xₙ, the equality ∑ᵢ xᵢ² = 0 implies xᵢ = 0 for every i.

**Problem.** In a formally real algebra, the relation x ≤ y, meaning that y − x is a sum of squares, is a partial order.

**How the definition helps.** Formal reality forces antisymmetry. If both differences are sums of squares, their sum is zero, so every squared element vanishes (our own). The zero square gives reflexivity, and concatenating sums gives transitivity (our own).

**nLab:** [formally real algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/formally+real+algebra), [Jordan algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jordan+algebra). It says: “The last condition (as in any formally real algebra) gives J a partial ordering: if we write x ≤ y when the element y − x is a sum of squares”

**Sources:**

- [Pascual Jordan, John von Neumann, Eugene Wigner, On an algebraic generalization of the quantum mechanical formalism, Annals of Mathematics 35 (1934) 29–64](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968117)
